implementation_notes: Swift's @inlinable exposes a declaration's body to the client's optimiser, which is the cross-module equivalent of C++ templates and is the only way to get cross-module inlining in a library - the Swift documentation is explicit that @inlinable is not appropriate for most functions because of the code-size cost and because it commits the body to the module's ABI. Swift otherwise inlines automatically via the optimiser (SILGen), and the diagnostic 'was not inlined' or the -Osize vs -O trade-off gives control. @_transparent is the internal, underscored form used inside the standard library for the smallest helpers (min/max/identity), and it substitutes the body at the call site like Kotlin's inline. The practical rule: apply @inlinable to small, performance-relevant cross-module functions and to generic constraints' witnesses; leave everything else to the optimiser.
idiom_name: @inlinable (cross-module body exposure); @_transparent (internal substitution); automatic optimiser inlining otherwise
pitfalls: @inlinable is not for most functions - the Swift docs say so explicitly; it costs code size and commits the body to the module's ABI (an ABI-stable library cannot change an @inlinable body without recompiling clients).
@_transparent is an underscored, non-public attribute intended for stdlib internals; using it in application code is unsupported and can change between compiler versions.
The release build uses -O (more inlining); the debug build does not, so an inlining measurement must be on release.
An inlinable generic function's witness must match across the module boundary or the client cannot inline it - an ABI mismatch silently disables the optimisation.
Exceeding the instruction cache with @inlinable makes a hot loop slower; profile the instruction footprint, not just one run's wall time.
